content_html_sanitized:
Posted November 8, 2000
Special to MarijuanaNews.com

First, the bad news:

In Alaska, we lost. The initiative there would not only have legalized marijuana for everyone over 18, but would have expunged the records of everyone previously convicted, and had other justifiable, but controversial provisions.

Nonetheless, it got almost 40% of the votes, and considering how far it went, and how much the state’s officials lied about it, that was not too bad a showing. We will see a more narrowly drawn Alaskan legalization initiative on the ballot in two years or less. We’ll be back!

As usual, the medical marijuana initiatives won.


In Nevada, where this was the second vote, as required by the state’s constitution, there was little opposition and Question 9 got 67.26% of the vote. In Colorado, where this was also the second vote, required by the late Secretary of State having hidden some of the petitions in her office, Amendment 20 passed with 53%. This was the narrowest margin of victory for a medical marijuana initiative, but it happened in the face of massive opposition from the state’s establishment, including the Denver Post.
See
Maine Passes Medical Marijuana Initiative By 61%
Against Almost Unanimous Establishment Opposition

While not directly related to marijuana, the victory for California’s Proposition 36 with 60.8% of the vote was a repudiation of the Drug War and the state establishment.

The proposal is expected to divert some 37,000 people a year from jails and prisons and put them into residential, clinical and other treatment programs in the community. The measure will take effect in July, 2001. It appropriates $120 million a year to provide the necessary treatment programs, but none of the money can be used for testing of offenders, which opponents contended is absolutely necessary to chart an addict's progress toward recovery.

It mandates treatment instead of jail or prison for first- or second-time non-violent drug offenders.

In Massachusetts, a very similar initiative, Question 8 failed with only 47% of the vote.

On the other hand, forfeiture reform bills won in

Utah with 68.9% of the vote. In Oregon forfeiture reform passed with 66% of the vote. Notice that conservative Utah approved forfeiture reform by a slightly wider margin than Oregon. This was not a " pro-drug " vote, but an anti-Drug War, pro-property rights vote.

Mendocino County Measure G allows up to 25 pot plants for personal use. It won with 58%. Basically, this is an attempt to get the narks out of people’s backyards.

Marijuana in the Massachusetts:

In the towns of Boxford, Georgetown, Hamilton, Ipswich, Manchester, and Wenham, there was a ballot question:

" Shall the representative of this district be instructed to introduce and vote for legislation that would make possession of marijuana a civil violation like a traffic ticket instead of a criminal offense, and require the police to hold a person under the age of eighteen cited for possession until released to a parent, guardian, or brought before a judge. "

It won in all of the towns, with around two thirds of the vote, over all.

It is clear from these results that the people of DEAland will take back their freedom from the Drug War.

Friday, MarijuanaNews.com will carry an exclusive analysis of the Bay State’s results by attorney Michael Cutler.
